title: The tablecloth
hookLine: Moses Isserles of Kraków adds Ashkenazi customs, called "the tablecloth"

lines: RICE ON ONE, NOT THE OTHER.
WHOSE PRACTICE IS IN THE BOOK?
cards: Passover in Kraków. On one family's table there is no rice, no beans, no lentils, though nothing in the Torah forbids them.
Far to the south, in Tzfat or Salonika, a Sephardic family may well be eating rice at the same seder. Both are keeping Passover. Both are following their parents.

So when a code of law arrives from Tzfat and says what Jews do, a rabbi in Kraków has a problem: whose practice does the book describe? His answer was not to throw the book away. It was to spread something over it.

teach.b: The rabbi was Moses Isserles of Kraków, known by his initials as the Rema. He had been working on his own long study of the same laws Karo had studied.
When the Shulchan Aruch appeared, he did not write a rival code. He wrote notes on it.

Wherever the customs of Ashkenaz, the Jews of Germany and Poland, differed from Karo's ruling, he added a short comment: this is our practice. He called those notes the Mappah, which means the tablecloth.
The joke is gentle and exact. Karo had set the table; Isserles spread a cloth over it, so it could be used in another house.
Printers later set his notes right inside Karo's text, in a different typeface, so one page held both.
The book that Sephardic and Ashkenazic Jews both use is a shared page with two voices on it, neither erasing the other. Behind the Mappah is a high respect for minhag, custom.
Isserles treated the practices of a community, handed down from parents, as something that carries weight in law, not as an afterthought.
Proverbs puts it simply: "forsake not the teaching of thy mother." Some readers have heard custom in that line, the things learned at home before anyone opened a book.
So when a Jewish practice is done one way in one family and another way next door, it may be neither mistake nor laziness. It may be the set table and the tablecloth, side by side.

how: Printed editions of the Shulchan Aruch include Isserles's notes inside Karo's text, and Ashkenazi Jews generally follow his rulings where they differ from Karo's, while Sephardic communities generally follow Karo.

games.q: you are a rabbi in Kraków. a new code from Tzfat doesn't match your community's customs. what do you do?
o: write your own code from scratch.
add notes where your custom differs.
games.why: Isserles wrote the Mappah, notes that spread a tablecloth over Karo's set table.

practice: Bring to mind a practice from someone else's family or community that you don't share: a holiday food, a way of greeting, the way they mourn or celebrate.
Instead of asking whether it's right, ask what it holds for them, whose hands taught it, and what it remembers.

wordCard.voice: The tablecloth. The Mappah, Moses Isserles's notes on the Shulchan Aruch, adding Ashkenazi custom so that one book could serve more than one community. Today's word.

orig.note: mappah means tablecloth: Isserles's name for his notes.
